description:
Hello, we are Penaburians! 

Just like the title suggests, our team consists a-mix-of Penabur students, combining our passion, skills, and aims into solving a certain mission regarding space.

In particular, we're highly motivated in fields such those of Astronomy, Robotics, Maths, Physics, Data Analytics, and Programming on how it seems to wavelessly intertwine through Arts, UI/UX Design, and 2D/3D Animation/Modelling.

We hope to gain experience and learn something new from our endeavors.
summary:
“Our launch slipped N days. Is our landing site still survivable, and what is the best alternative site or date?” MOON SLIP answers that question in seconds.

We chose 11 landing sites and precomputed where the Sun and Earth sit relative to the local horizon every hour for a full year. We used NASA JPL’s DE421 ephemeris, and NASA LRO LOLA elevation data for real terrain skylines at the polar sites. The planner turns this into a Green, Yellow or Red verdict from a visible, adjustable formula covering sunlight for power, the longest darkness, and direct-to-Earth communication. It shows the slip margin, the next good landing window and the best alternative site, with a calendar of sites against dates and charts of the Sun and Earth above the horizon. An interactive 3D Moon shows all 11 sites coloured by verdict, lit by the real Sun position, and plays through the mission.

Every number is checked: our Sun and Earth positions match NASA JPL Horizons to within 0.02°, and our terrain heights match NASA values to within 6 m.

When a launch slips, MOON SLIP shows whether a mission still works, and where to go instead.
details:
What it does
MOON SLIP answers one question in seconds: “Our launch slipped N days. Is our landing site still survivable, and what is the best alternative site or date?” Pick a landing site, a planned landing date and the number of days of slip. The site returns a Green, Yellow or Red verdict, the slip margin (how many more days the landing can slip before it turns Red), the next good landing window, and the best alternative site on the same date. A calendar shows all 11 sites against every landing date at once. Clicking a cell opens charts of the Sun’s and Earth’s height above the real horizon during the mission, with the longest darkness, sunlit fraction, Earth-visible fraction and the time to the next sunset and Earthset.

An interactive 3D Moon shows all 11 sites coloured by their verdict on the slipped date, lit by the Sun’s real position from our data, with Earth shown in its direction. Users can play or scrub through the mission to watch the Sun and Earth move, turn and zoom the Moon, jump to the south pole, the near side or the selected site, and click a site to select it. A readout gives the Sun’s and Earth’s height at the site against the local terrain limit, for example “Sun 3.29° (limit 0.93°), sunlit”. Up to four scenarios can also be compared side by side.

How it works
We precomputed where the Sun and Earth sit in the sky at each site, every hour for a full year (1 Dec 2026 to 30 Nov 2027), using NASA JPL’s DE421 ephemeris and NASA NAIF lunar orientation data. This includes the Moon’s wobble (libration). For the five sites near the south pole, we used NASA LRO LOLA elevation data to compute the real terrain skyline in 360 directions, because ridges and craters there block the low Sun. The verdict comes from a visible, adjustable formula: is the Sun up at landing, is the longest darkness short enough for the lander, and is Earth visible for direct communication.

Why it matters
Missions rarely keep their dates, and at the lunar south pole a few days or a kilometre can decide whether a lander has power and contact with Earth. Real terrain cuts the sunlight at IM-1’s landing site from 49% to 34% of the year. Our tool helps planners respond quickly to delays, and shows students and the public why lunar landing is so demanding.

Accuracy
We checked our numbers against independent NASA sources. 18 of 18 Sun and Earth positions agree with NASA JPL Horizons to within 0.019°. Our ground heights agree with NASA’s published value and LROC QuickMap to within 6 m.

Tools
Python with Skyfield and NumPy in Google Colab for the calculations. HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the website, with three.js for the 3D Moon. Figma for design, Netlify for hosting. The code was written with AI assistance (Claude by Anthropic), and the design was generated with Figma AI. The team directed, ran and checked all of it. No data value was generated by AI.

Creativity and factors we considered
Instead of another Sun-and-Earth viewer, we built around the moment planners actually face: a delay. We kept the formula visible and adjustable, labelled every limit honestly, and made the site run with no server, so it loads instantly and cannot fail during judging. Verdicts use letters as well as colours, for colour-blind users. Known limits: one-hour time steps, terrain only near the south pole, and no slope assessment.
